The kettle had been screaming for a while before Nadia noticed it.

"You were going to tell me about Thursday," Ruth said. She had not moved
from the doorway.

"I was going to—" Nadia turned off the gas. The screaming thinned out and
stopped. "I was going to, yes."

"But."

"But then Dad called and it stopped being a thing I could say out loud."

Ruth came in and sat down at the table without being asked, which was how
she had always done it, and which had annoyed their mother for thirty
years. She turned one of the cold mugs a quarter turn. Then another
quarter.

"He told me a different version," she said.

"He would."

"No, listen. He told me you asked him first. In March." Ruth looked up.
"Did you?"

Nadia stood with her back to the stove and counted the tiles above the
sink, the way she had counted them at nine, at fifteen, at twenty-six with
a suitcase in the hall.

"There were reasons," she said.

"I'm not asking for reasons. I'm asking if you did."

Outside, someone's car alarm started and gave up.
